title: Winnipegger facing extradition over COVID relief fraud, money laundering allegations
summary: A Winnipeg man is facing extradition after U.S. authorities accused him of defrauding a pandemic-era relief program of hundreds of thousands of dollars.

image.caption: Ajay Singh of Winnipeg is facing extradition to the U.S. on allegations he was involved in a scheme to defraud a COVID-19 relief program in that country. (Realtor.ca)

blocks.text: Manitoba
A Winnipeg man is facing extradition after U.S. authorities accused him of defrauding a pandemic-era relief program of hundreds of thousands of dollars.
Ajay Singh, 46, used fake payroll numbers for forgivable loans through pandemic-era program, U.S. says

Ajay Singh, a 46-year-old Canadian citizen, was arrested last December on allegations he was part of a bank fraud and money laundering scheme to get funds meant to help small businesses pay workers during the COVID-19 pandemic.

U.S. officials accused Singh of using inflated or fake payroll numbers to successfully apply for more than $11.5 million US in forgivable loans, according to an extradition request submitted by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Wisconsin.
The lender, Wells Fargo, was able to recover most of the money, but more than $600,000 US was unaccounted for, the document said.
The request did not mention any specific charges Singh — also known as Ajay Singh Kalkat — would face in the U.S. A final decision on whether he should be extradited is pending.

The man had asked courts to stop the proceedings, arguing Canadian authorities violated his Charter rights by issuing an arrest warrant without knowing what he would be charged with. A Manitoba Court of King's Bench judge dismissed that application in September.
The extradition request "contained detailed descriptions of the conduct underlying these allegations, including the names of witnesses and documents," Justice Ami Kotler wrote in the decision.

"This does not mean that Mr. Singh is not entitled to know what charges he is facing in the United States," Kotler said. "But the failure to identify these charges in the warrant application did not, in my view, represent a violation of Mr. Singh's [Charter] rights."

items: 3rd person charged in alleged $11M scheme to defraud Ontario COVID-19 relief fund

blocks.text: The U.S. extradition request said Singh applied to the federal COVID Paycheck Protection Program (PPP) 19 times through three Wisconsin-based companies between 2020 and 2021: Aikam Logistics, AK Hunt Capital Finance LLC and AK Hunt Ltd.
Four of the applications were approved, the document said.

Trucking company Aikam Logistics was granted a $301,882 US loan in 2020 for payroll purposes, with Singh submitting documents that said it had 10 employees. U.S. authorities allege only about $5,000 US appeared to have been spent on items that could possibly be business related.
A year later, Singh submitted another loan application for Aikam, with documents saying the company had 97 employees, the extradition request said. Aikam received a loan for $997,000 US.
Some companies 'existed only on paper,' officials say
Officials pointed to inconsistencies in the number of employees Singh reported to have in 2020 compared with 2021.
The U.S. document also contains allegations the two other companies owned by Singh "existed only on paper in that they did not pay employees or earn revenue."
AK Hunt received a $301,882 US loan based on an application saying it had nine employees in 2020.
AK Hunt Capital Finance LLC. received a $9,975,000 US loan in 2021. The application said the company had 497 employees.
The documents say a witness would be able to testify in court that the office listed as the address for AK Hunt Capital Finance was not large enough to host that many employees.
The witness could say Singh was renting the space for about half a year, paying $450 US a month, officials said.

blocks.text: Wells Fargo began closing business accounts linked to those companies after approving the $9.9-million US loan in March 2021. The document said several identical applications had previously been rejected.
The document said Singh sent a letter to the bank agreeing to reverse the last loan in April 2021 after being interviewed by a Wells Fargo investigator.
"It has come to my attention that the PPP funds should not be used for the purposes I intended," the letter said.
Singh did not address the other loans that were approved, U.S. officials said.
Thousands spent on jewelry, document says

The extradition request said an Internal Revenue Service investigator would be able to give testimony about several transactions that took place after each of the loans was granted, including transfers to broker and personal accounts in multiple banks, as well as cashier cheque purchases.
The investigator had also traced about $15,000 US of the money in jewelry purchases for Singh's wife, the document said.
Kotler said in the September decision the allegations outlined in the U.S. request would have carried a maximum jail sentence of 14 years under Canada's Criminal Code.
An RCMP officer said in an affidavit it was in the public interest to issue the arrest warrant.
Singh was granted bail under several conditions in December, including that he surrender his passport to police.
He was also barred from having sole authority for financial transactions or loans as part of his employment.
The inspector general for the U.S. Small Business Administration estimated more than $200 billion US in COVID-19 aid was potentially fraudulent, including $64 billion US in PPP loan funds.
CBC News tried to contact Singh, but he was not immediately available.
The United States Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Wisconsin declined to comment.
